content: Dr. Aruna Dewan is associated with the Center for Education, Awareness, and Research on Chemicals and Health in Ahmedabad, India. Her expertise lies in clinical toxicology, analytical toxicology, and lead poisoning caused by traditional remedies. She has not declared any conflicts of interest, and no action is required in this regard. Dr. Thuppil Venkatesh is affiliated with the National Referral Centre for Lead Poisoning in India, located at St. John’s National Academy of Health Sciences in Bangalore, India. He has not declared any conflicts of interest, and no action is required. Dr. Yona Amitai, from the Department of Management at Bar Ilan University in Ramat Gan, Israel, specializes in pediatric toxicology, injury and poison prevention, and children’s environmental health. No conflicts of interest have been declared, and no issues were identified concerning the development of the guideline. Professor Paul Dargan, a Consultant Physician and Professor of Clinical Toxicology at Guy’s and St. Thomas’ NHS Foundation Trust in London, United Kingdom, focuses on clinical toxicology and the management of lead poisoning in low-resource settings. No conflicts of interest were identified concerning the development of the guideline. Dr. Natalie Thurtle, previously a Health Advisor for the Zamfara Heavy Metal Poisoning project with Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in Amsterdam, Netherlands, is now based at St. George’s Hospital in Sydney, Australia. Her expertise includes clinical toxicology, medicine in low-resource settings, and the management of lead poisoning in such environments. She was employed by MSF as a long-term consultant during the lead poisoning outbreak in Zamfara, Nigeria, where she led initial response activities. She is also a co-author of a paper detailing the outcomes of a humanitarian intervention providing chelation therapy to children in Zamfara. No conflicts of interest were identified concerning the development of the guideline. Lead concentration in breast milk and the mobilization of lead from bone in women are considered important factors. These include gastrointestinal decontamination after ingestion of solid lead objects, chelation therapy for children with elevated blood lead concentrations, and chelation therapy for adolescents or adults with elevated blood lead levels.
